text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Miroshnychenko v. Antufeay,

2021 BCSC 1531

Date: 20210806

Docket:
S2058710

Registry: Prince George

Between:

Oleksandr
Miroshnychenko, for Miro Chembiotech Ltd.

Plaintiff

And

Dale Antufeay, Ken Bitschy, and Dean Miller for Houle Electric
Limited

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice Tindale

Reasons for Judgment

In Chambers

The plaintiff appearing

by teleconference:

O.
Miroshnychenko

Counsel for the defendants,

appearing by teleconference:

T.S.
Galbraith

Place and Date of Hearing:

Prince
George, B.C.

April
8, 2021

Place and Date of Judgment:

Prince
George, B.C.

August
6, 2021

[
1
]

The defendants Dale Antufeay, Ken Bitschy, Dean
Miller (the “Individual Defendants”) and Houle Electric Limited pursuant to a
Notice of Application filed March 22, 2021 seek an order that the Notice of
Civil Claim filed in this proceeding on December 8, 2020 be struck out pursuant
to Rule 9- 5 (1) of the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
.

[
2
]

The plaintiff Oleksandr Miroshnychenko, for Miro
Chembiotech Ltd. (“MCL”) opposes the application.

Background

[
3
]

Oleksandr Miroshnychenko is the owner of MCL.

[
4
]

The plaintiff MCL is a company engaged in the
production of amino acid chelated minerals and Zinc Lysinate.

[
5
]

Houle Electric Limited (“Houle”) is a company
incorporated pursuant to the laws of British Columbia.

[
6
]

Ken Bitschy is a director of Houle.

[
7
]

Dale Antufeay is an employee of Houle.

[
8
]

Dean Miller is an employee of Houle.

[
9
]

The plaintiff on or about June 14, 2019 showed
equipment to Houle that it wanted connected in a premises.

[
10
]

Houle attended at the premises during the week of October 5 - 12,
2019 to connect the equipment. On October 31, 2019 Houle attended at the
premises to complete the installation of the equipment however that installation
was not completed.

[
11
]

On December 8, 2020 the plaintiff filed a Notice of Claim.

[
12
]

On December 23, 2020 the defendants filed a Response to Civil Claim.

[
13
]

On January 27, 2021 the defendants issued a demand for particulars
to the plaintiff as well as a letter setting out substantive defects in the
Notice of Civil Claim.

[
14
]

On February 9, 2021 the plaintiff issued a response to the demand
for particulars and on February 10, 2021 the plaintiffs provided a response to
the letter of the defendants setting out the defects in the Notice of Civil
Claim.

Position of the Parties

Defendants

[
15
]

The defendants seek to have the Notice of Civil Claim struck out in
its entirety because they argue that is so prolix and confusing it is
impossible to understand the case to be met.

[
16
]

The defendants argue that the plaintiff has filed a Notice of Civil
Claim relying on the
Class Proceedings Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996 c. 50 however
there is no basis to bring such an action. The Notice of Civil Claim discloses
no reasonable cause of action under the
Class Proceedings Act
.

[
17
]

The defendants also argue that the plaintiff has brought a claim
pursuant to the
Business Practices and Consumer Protection Act
, S.B.C.
2004, c 2 (“
BPCPA
”) however the plaintiff has not pleaded that they
entered into a contract for personal, family or household purposes with any of
the defendants as required by
s. 1
of the
BPCPA
.

[
18
]

In addition the defendants argue that the plaintiff has acknowledged
that this was a commercial transaction between the parties.

[
19
]

The defendants argue that Mr. Miroshnychenko is named as a plaintiff
however no claims are pleaded against any of the defendants on his behalf. Mr. Miroshnychenko
acknowledges that he is not a personal plaintiff but says he represents MCL.

[
20
]

The defendants also argue that there are no claims pleaded against
any of the Individual Defendants and any claims against them should be struck
out. Mr. Miroshnychenko acknowledges that the action is not against the Individual
Defendants.

[
21
]

The defendants argue that the plaintiff’s allegation of breach of
contract does not contain the necessary facts, particulars and circumstances to
found a cause of action in contract. The pleadings contain irrelevant facts and
arguments. The defendants argue that the breach of contract pleadings should be
struck.

[
22
]

The defendants argue that the fraudulent misrepresentation claim by
the plaintiff does not allege any specific representation made by any of the
defendants which they intended the plaintiff to act on or to induce the
plaintiff to enter into a contract.

[
23
]

The defendants note that the plaintiff alleges that the fraudulent
misrepresentation was made in December 2019 through the submission of an
invoice by Houle to MCL for work already performed.

[
24
]

The defendants concede that there may be a claim for breach of
contract and it is in this area that leave to amend the Notice of Civil Claim could
be granted.

[
25
]

The defendants also seek special costs against the plaintiff because
they argue that the plaintiff has been persistent in bringing spurious claims
that have no merit.

Plaintiff

[
26
]

The plaintiff argues that when the defendants provided an invoice
dated July 10, 2019 they had entered into a contract for the connection of equipment
to the electrical distribution board. The plaintiff argues that that the Notice
of Civil Claim outlines the manner in which the defendants breached the duties
they had under the contract.

[
27
]

The plaintiff argues that the remedy for breach of contract can be
monetary damages, an injunction or specific performance.

[
28
]

The plaintiff argues that when Mr. Antufeay demanded payment on
behalf of Houle he was providing false or misleading information. This appears
to be the basis for the plaintiff’s claim in fraudulent misrepresentation.

[
29
]

The plaintiff argues that Mr. Miroshnychenko only speaks on behalf
of MCL and the Notice of Civil Claim did not refer to “plaintiffs” in the
plural.

[
30
]

The plaintiff argues that the Individual Defendants were named
because if a corporation commits an offence under the
BPCPA
an employee,
officer, director or agent of the corporation can also commit an offence.

[
31
]

The plaintiff seeks full compensation for its losses.

[
32
]

The plaintiff argues that the defendants’ Notice of Application
should be dismissed.

Decision

[
33
]

Rule 3-1 of the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
reads:

(2) A notice of civil claim must do the
following:

(a) set out a
concise statement of the material facts giving rise to the claim;

(b) set out the
relief sought by the plaintiff against each named defendant;

(c) set out a
concise summary of the legal basis for the relief sought;

…

[
34
]

Rule 3-7 of the
Supreme Court Civil Rules

reads:

(1) A pleading must not contain the evidence
by which the facts alleged in it are to be proved.

…

(6) A party must not plead an allegation of
fact or a new ground or claim inconsistent with the parties previous pleading.

…

(18) If the
party pleading relies on misrepresentation, fraud, breach of trust, wilful
default or undue influence, or if particulars may be necessary, full
particulars, with dates and items if applicable, must be stated in the
pleading.

[
35
]

In
Delaney & Friends Cartoon Productions
Ltd. v. Radical Entertainment Inc
.
et al
.
2005 BCSC 371
Joyce J. in
reviewing the jurisprudence pertaining to the basic function of pleadings
stated the following at para. 8:

In
Homalco Indian Band v. British
Columbia
(1998),
1998 CanLII 6658 (BC SC)
, 25 C.P.C. (4th) 107, [1998] B.C.J. No. 2703 (S.C.) (cited
to C.P.C.) at pp. 109-110, K. Smith J. (as he then was) summarized the basic
function of pleadings:

The ultimate
function of pleadings is to clearly define the issues of fact and law to be
determined by the court. The issues must be defined for each cause of action
relied upon by the plaintiff. That process is begun by the plaintiff stating,
for each cause, the material facts, that is, those facts necessary for the
purpose of formulating a complete cause of action:
Troup v. McPherson
(1965),

1965 CanLII 767 (BC SC)
, 53 W.W.R. 37 (B.C.S.C.) at 39. …

A useful description of the proper structure
of a plea of a cause of action as set out in J.H. Koffler and A. Reppy
,
Handbook of Common Law Pleading
, (St. Paul, Minn.: West Publishing Co.,
1969) at p. 85:

Of course the
essential elements of any claim of relief or remedial right will vary from
action to action. But, on analysis, the pleader will find that the facts
prescribed by the substandard of law as necessary to constitute a cause of
action in a given case, may be classified under three heads: (1) The
plaintiff’s right or title; (2) The defendant’s wrongful act violating that
right or title; (3) the consequent damage, whether nominal or substantial. And,
of course, the facts constituting the cause of action should be stated with
certainty and precision, and in their natural order, so as to disclose the
three elements essential to every cause of action, to wit, the right, the
wrongful act and the damage.

If the statement
of claim is to serve the ultimate purpose of pleadings, the material facts of
each cause of action relied upon should be set out in the above manner. As
well, they should be stated succinctly and the particulars should follow and
should be identified as such:
Gittings v. Caneco Audio-Publishers Inc
.
(1988),
1988 CanLII 2832 (BC CA)
, 26 B.C.L.R. (2d) 349 (B.C.C.A.) at 353.

[
36
]

The defendants argue that the Notice of Civil Claim does not clearly
define the issues of fact and law to be determined by the court. The defendants
say that the Notice of Civil Claim is difficult to understand.

[
37
]

Rule 9-5 of the
Supreme Court Civil Rules

reads:

At any stage of the proceeding, the court
may order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of a pleading,
petition or other document on the ground that

a)

it discloses no reasonable claim or defence, as the case may be,

b)

it is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

c)

it may prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing of
the proceeding, or

d)

it is otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court may pronounce judgment or
order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may order the costs of the
application to be paid as special costs.

…

[
38
]

The test for striking a claim pursuant to Rule
9-5 (1) and the applicable jurisprudence was summarized by Burnyeat J. in
Gateway
Building Management Limited v. Manjit Singh Randhawa

2013 BCSC 350
at paras.

16 and 17
:

[16] The test to be applied to determine
whether an action should be struck out as disclosing no reasonable claim
requires a conclusion that, assuming that the facts as stated or even if
amended our true, those facts disclose no cause of action, the pleadings
disclose no arguable issue, and it is plain and obvious that the claim cannot
succeed…

[17] In
Dempsey v. Envision Credit Union
,

2006 BCSC 750
, Garson J., as she then was, provided the following summary of
Rule 9-5 jurisprudence:

In summary, a pleading will be struck out
if:

a)

the pleadings are unintelligible, confusing and difficult to
understand (
Citizens for Foreign aid Reform, [Citizens of Foreign Aid Reform
Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4th) 266 (B.C.S.C.)]);

b)

the pleadings do not establish a cause of action and do not advance
a claim known in law (
Citizens for Foreign aid Reform, supra
);

c)

the pleadings are without substance in that they are groundless,
fanciful and trifle with the Courts time (
Borsato v. Basra
, [
2000 BCSC 28 (CanLII)
, [2000]
B.C.J. No. 84 (S.C.)])

d)

the pleadings are not bona fides, are oppressive and are designed to
cause the Defendants anxiety, trouble and expense (
Borsato v. Basra
, supra
);

e)

the action is brought for an improper purpose, particularly the
harassment and of session of the Defendants (
Ebrahim v. Ebrahim
,
2002
BCSC 466
).

(at para. 17)

[
39
]

There are a number of problems with the Notice of Civil Claim filed
on December 8, 2020. Some of those are conceded by the plaintiff.

[
40
]

For instance Mr. Miroshnychenko concedes that he did not intend
that he be a plaintiff but rather he speaks on behalf of MCL. Upon a review of
the Notice of Civil Claim there are no claims made by Mr. Miroshnychenko in his
personal capacity. The pleadings do not establish a cause of action on behalf
of Mr. Miroshnychenko and his name in the style of cause is struck out. In the
Notice of Civil Claim para. 4 refers to Mr. Miroshnychenko as the plaintiff
however I will allow him to amend this paragraph to properly describe the
plaintiff as MCL.

[
41
]

In addition the Notice of Civil Claim purports to be brought “In the
Provincial Court of British Columbia”. That is clearly an error and I will
allow the plaintiff to amend the Notice of Civil Claim to reflect that this
action has been brought in the Supreme Court of British Columbia.

[
42
]

The Notice of Civil Claim also purports to be “
Brought under the
Class Proceedings Act
,
R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 50
”. The pleadings do not
establish a cause of action which could be brought under this act and as I
understand the plaintiff’s submissions he is not bringing a class-action
lawsuit against the defendants. This portion of the Notice of Civil Claim is
struck out.

[
43
]

The Notice of Civil Claim includes as defendants
the Individual Defendants. The plaintiff in a document filed on February 10,
2020 purporting to respond to inquiries by the defendants stated the following
at paras. 2 and 4:

(2) The action is not against the personal
defendants Mr. Dale Antufeay, Mr. Ken Bitschy or Mr. Dean Miller but against
Houle Electric Limited. The defendant in the action “Dale Antufeay, Ken Bitschy
and Dean Miller for Houle Electric Limited” means that Mr. Dale Antufeay, or
Mr. Ken Bitschy or Mr. Dean Miller acts “for” or “on behalf of” Houle electric
Limited, but not as personal plaintiff. For example, all invoices or Final
Demand Collection Notice were presented by Mr. Muller, Mr. Andre Desgange, or
Mr. Dale Antufeay as Service Electrician, or Service manager, or Credit &
Collection Specialist of Houle Electric Limited, but not as individual contractor.
Mr. Ken Bitschy represents Houle Electric Limited as Director of BC Registry
Service during our personal meeting, assuring that he will personally determine
the reason the spray dryer and fluid bed dryer are not connected to the
electric control panel.

…

(4) This was a
commercial transaction between Mirochembiotech and Houle Electric Limited.

[
44
]

The plaintiff’s argument is that Houle is vicariously liable for the
action of their employees. There is however no claims made against any of the
Individual Defendants in the Notice of Civil Claim.

[
45
]

The plaintiff argues that there has been a breach of the
BPCPA

on behalf of the defendants and that under that
Act
Houle can be liable
for the action of their employees

[
46
]

The
BPCPA
defines a consumer transaction
in
s. 1
as:

a)

a supply of goods or services or real property by a supplier to a
consumer for purposes that are primarily personal, family or household, or

b)

a solicitation, offer, advertisement or promotion by a supplier with
respect to a transaction referred to in paragraph (a), and, except in Parts 4
and 5, includes a solicitation of a consumer by a supplier for a contribution
of money or other property by the consumer.

[
47
]

In
A Speedy Solutions Oil Tank Removal Inc.
v. Garraway
,
2019 BCSC 1091
Jenkins J. reviewed the applicable case law
regarding a consumer transaction under the
BPCPA
at paras. 74 - 78:

[74] The authorities rightly rely on the
plain wording of the
BPCPA
and the purpose of the
BPCPA
. The
court in
Miller v. Merck Frosst Canada Ltd
.,
2013 BCSC 544
, aff’d
2015
BCCA 353
, said:

79   The purpose
of the
BPCPA
is to protect consumers. It is to be broadly construed to
carry out that purpose and is to be interpreted generously in favour of
consumers (
Seidal v. Telus Communications Inc.
,
2011 SCC 15 (CanLII)
, [2011] 1 S.C.R. 531 (S.C.C.)
at para.
37
;
Stanway v. Wyeth Canada Inc
.,
2012 BCCA 260
(B.C.C.A.) at
paras.
78 and 79
).

[75] Whether or not a transaction is a
“consumer transaction” turns on the purpose of the consumer who is engaging in
the transaction: See
Webster v. Robbins Parking Service Ltd
.,
2016 BCSC
1863
at para.
44
.

[76] In
Nanaimo Shipyards Ltd. v. Keith
,

2008 BCSC 1150
at para.
57
[
Nanaimo Shipyards
], the court stated:

… It is not
whether the provider of services is a commercial operation. It is whether the
purchaser is an individual purchasing for primarily personal, family or
household purposes. The three words “personal, family or household” are
disjunctive, and although the Breanna was a very large item, I would expect
most people to think of it as personal, and for family or household purposes as
opposed to commercial use.

[77] In
Nanaimo Shipyards
, Dr. Keith
had contracted with the plaintiff for the rescue and repair of his 72-foot
motor vessel which had run aground.

[78] In
Van
Beek v. Dodd
,
2010 BCSC 1639
, the defendant was at all material times a
real estate agent and developer, building a house to be the plaintiff’s primary
residence. The court found this to be a “primarily personal, family or
household” purpose. Referring to
Nanaimo Shipya
rds, the court found the
defendant was “actively involved in the transaction and, thus, is a “supplier”
within the meaning of the [
BPCPA
]”.

[
48
]

Based on the evidence that I have before me, the plaintiffs own
characterization that this was a commercial transaction between the plaintiff
and Houle and the fact that the Notice of Civil Claim discloses no cause of
action relating to a personal, family or household purposes it is plain and
obvious that that a claim against the Individual Defendants will not succeed.
They will be struck from the Notice of Civil Claim as defendants. I will also
strike paras. 5 - 7 from the Notice of Civil Claim which refers to the
Individual Defendants.

[
49
]

In addition as the impugned transaction between the plaintiff and
the defendant Houle was a commercial transaction. The
BPCPA
is not applicable
and I strike out paras. 31 - 33 of the Notice of Civil Claim. In addition I
strike out paras. 1 and 2 under the heading Relief Sought in the Notice of
Civil Claim because it is plain and obvious that an argument pursuant to the
BPCPA

will not succeed.

[
50
]

The plaintiff also makes a claim for fraudulent misrepresentation
which appears to be based on the plaintiff’s allegation that an invoice
supplied by Houle was false and misleading.

[
51
]

The British Columbia Court of
Appeal
in Wang
v. Shao

2019 BCCA 130
reviewed the elements of a fraudulent
misrepresentation at para. 24:

[24] The trial Judge then turned to Ms.
Shao’s claim for fraudulent misrepresentation. It is trite law that fraudulent
misrepresentation involves the following elements that must be proven by the
claimant:

(a) the wrongdoer
must make a representation of fact to the victim;

(b) the
representation must be faults in fact;

(c) the party
making the representation must have known the representation was false at the
time it was made;

(d) the
misrepresentor must have intended the victim act on the representation; and

(e) the victim must have been induced to
enter into the contract in reliance upon it.

[
52
]

In this case the plaintiff alleges that the fraudulent
misrepresentation was made after the contract was entered into between the
parties. The misrepresentation was in relationship to an invoice that was
presented to the plaintiff. The Notice of Civil Claim does not support a cause of
action in fraudulent misrepresentation because the plaintiff could not have
been induced to enter into the contract as the alleged misrepresentation was
made after the contract was entered into.

[
53
]

I will strike out paras. 10, 29 and 30 from the Notice of Civil
Claim as it is plain and obvious that they do not support a cause of action in
relationship to a claim for fraudulent misrepresentation. In addition under the
heading Relief Sought I will strike paragraph 6 as it relates to fraudulent
misrepresentation.

[
54
]

The plaintiff also seeks punitive damages from the defendants based
primarily on the claim for fraudulent misrepresentation. It is plain and
obvious that this argument will not succeed and I strike out the claim for
punitive damages from the Notice of Civil Claim.

[
55
]

The breach of contract allegations in the Notice of Civil Claim at paras.
8, 9, and 11 - 27 are confusing and hard to understand. In my view it is not
however plain and obvious that the claim for breach of contract will not
succeed. I do not find that the allegation of breach of contract by the
plaintiff is frivolous or vexatious and I would allow the plaintiff to amend
these paragraphs.

[
56
]

Under the heading Legal Basis paras. 1, 2, and 3 relate to the
allegation of breach of contract however they lack specificity as to the nature
of the contract and parameters of the contract. I will however allow the
plaintiff to amend these paragraphs as it is not plain and obvious that the
claim for breach of contract will fail.

[
57
]

Finally under the heading Relief Sought paras. 4 and 7 are confusing
however they relate to the allegation of breach of contract. I will allow the
plaintiff to amend these paragraphs.

[
58
]

The plaintiff will have 60 days from service upon him of these
reasons to amend, file and serve his amended pleadings in relationship to the
breach of contract allegations.

Conclusion

[
59
]

In conclusion I will make the following orders:

•

The reference to Mr. Miroshnychenko as a
plaintiff is struck out from the Notice of Civil Claim filed on December 8,
2020 without leave to amend.

•

The reference to the
Class Proceedings Act

in the Notice of Civil Claim filed on December 8, 2020 is struck out without
leave to amend.

•

The reference to Dale Antufeay, Ken Bitschy and
Dean Miller as defendants are struck out from the Notice of Civil Claim filed on
December 8, 2020 as well as paras. 5 - 7 without leave to amend. In addition
any claim against the Individual Defendants is dismissed.

•

The plaintiff’s claim for fraudulent misrepresentation
is dismissed. Paragraphs 10, 29 and 30 of the Notice of Civil Claim filed on
December 8, 2020 are struck out without leave to amend. In addition para. 6
under the heading Relief Sought is struck out without leave to amend.

•

The plaintiff’s claim pursuant to the
BPCPA

is dismissed. Paragraphs 31 -33 of the Notice of Civil Claim filed on December
8, 2020 are struck out without leave to amend. In addition paras. 1 and 2 under
the heading Relief Sought are struck out without leave to amend.

•

The plaintiff’s claim for punitive damages is
dismissed.

•

The plaintiff has leave to amend the Notice of
Civil Claim filed on December 8, 2020 to reflect that this action has been
brought in the Supreme Court of British Columbia.

•

The plaintiff has leave to amend the following
paras. in the Notice of Civil Claim filed on December 8, 2020:

i.

Paras. 4, 8, 9 and 11 - 27;

ii.

Under the heading Legal Basis paras. 1, 2 and 3;
and

iii.

Under the heading Relief Sought paras. 4 and 7.

•

The plaintiff will have 60 days from service
upon him of these reasons to amend, file and serve his amended pleadings.

Costs

[
60
]

The defendants pursuant to Rule 9-5 (1) seek an award of special
costs. The defendants say that the plaintiff was persistent in bringing
spurious claims, alleging fraud with no basis and refusing to withdraw such
claims. The defendants argue that this conduct is worthy of rebuke of the
court.

[
61
]

Mr. Miroshnychenko is a self-represented litigant. While there are
significant problems with the manner in which the Notice of Civil Claim was
drafted I do not find that his intention was to bring meritless claims for an
improper purpose or abuse the courts process.

[
62
]

In the circumstances I declined to make an award
for special costs.

[
63
]

The defendants were however successful and they shall have their
costs Appendix B, Scale B pursuant to the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
.

“The Honourable
Mr. Justice Tindale”
